lines.en: The Blue Rivers. The main band comes on at nine.

lines.en: Cool! **I love** the main band. **I’m a big fan of** their drummer.

lines.en: Me too! **Have you ever been to** one of their shows?
lines.pt: Eu também! Você já foi a algum show deles?

lines.en: No, this is **my first show**. And you?

pages.title: Music and Live Shows

situation.text: You arrive at a concert and talk to a stranger in line. You ask who is playing, share the music you love and ask if he has been to other shows.

pages.goal: By the end of the class you can talk about music you love, ask who is playing, ask about past experiences and make small talk at a concert.
canDo: Say what you love: I love… / I’m a big fan of…
Ask: Have you ever been to…?
Answer with: Yes, twice / No, never

I ask about a past experience.
I keep the small talk going.

pages.title: Cultural snapshot — Live music in the USA
pages.intro: Live music is a big part of social life in the USA, from small bars to big festivals. Look and guess before you read.

cards.note: Many concert venues limit bag size, and some only allow clear bags. Check the rules before you go.
At slow songs, fans often lift their phone lights and sway to the music.
After the last song, the crowd claps and cheers. The band comes back for one or two more songs: the encore.

levels.A2: The band plays one or two more songs after the show.
levels.B1: After the main set, the crowd cheers until the band returns for an encore.
levels.B2: The encore is a shared ritual: the audience calls the band back, and artists often save a favorite song for it.

qs.q: How do you protect your ears at a loud show?
qs.pt: Como proteger os ouvidos em um show alto?

levels.A2: You can wear earplugs. They lower the noise.
levels.B1: Many fans wear earplugs, which lower the volume but keep the music clear.
levels.B2: Earplugs made for music reduce the volume without ruining the sound, and many regular concertgoers carry a pair.

qs.q: What is good manners at a show?
qs.pt: O que é educação em um show?

levels.A2: Do not push and do not block the view.
levels.B1: Keep your phone down during songs if people are behind you, and respect personal space.
levels.B2: In a crowd, respecting space and sightlines matters more than anything: it keeps the experience good for everyone.

pages.compare: In Brazil crowds often sing every word and dance together. In the USA fans also sing along, and they often wait for the encore. Is there a custom at shows where you live?

pages.title: Pronunciation lab — natural American English
pages.tip: Music words have vowels that are easy to confuse: “love” (/ʌ/), “loud” (/aʊ/), “band” (/æ/). Open your mouth for /æ/ and relax for /ʌ/.

own.prompt: Write a sentence with “love” or “loud” about music you like.
own.criteria: Say it twice. Is “love” short and relaxed, and “loud” long and open?

teach.goal: UM só fenômeno: Key vowel sounds.

Modele devagar e normal; peça que o estudante bata palmas na sílaba forte.
group: Coro, depois duplas; circule ouvindo.
Cada estudante cria uma frase própria.

pages.title: Level up — the same situation from A1 to C2
pages.intro: You do not need six different methods: the structure stays, while language complexity and autonomy grow.

ladder.goal: Say what you love with short phrases.

ladder.say: I love this band. Have you ever seen them live?
ladder.goal: Share taste and ask about experience.

ladder.say: I’ve been a fan of this band for years, but I’ve never seen them live.
Seeing them live had been on my list for ages, so I jumped at the chance when tickets came out.
Their live shows are said to be a different experience altogether, and I can see why people rave about them.
It’s one of those rare shows where the crowd and the band seem to breathe together.

pages.note: This progression is illustrative: complex sentences do not define a level on their own. CEFR also considers comprehension, autonomy, fluency, accuracy, interaction and appropriateness.
